cards.front: Recall a key point about Risalah: Prophethood
cards.back: Muslims believe Allah sent prophets (rasul and nabi) to every nation to guide people to the truth. All prophets brought the same message: worship one God and live righteously. Muhammad is the final and greatest prophet — the "Seal of the Prophets" (Surah 33:40).

cards.front: What should you know about rs exam tips — risalah: prophethood?
cards.back: 1. For Risalah: Prophethood questions, always include specific scriptural or source references where relevant 2. Explain both religious and non-religious viewpoints 3. Use specialist vocabulary precisely (e.g. terms from the specification) 4. Evaluate by analysing strengths and weaknesses of different views before reaching your conclusion 5. Link your discussion of Risalah: Prophethood to its real-world impact on believers and society

cards.front: What should you know about uk context?
cards.back: The stories of the prophets are central to Muslim religious education in Britain. Madrasahs (Islamic schools) teach children about the lives and teachings of all the major prophets, emphasising their patience, courage and devotion to Allah.

cards.front: What should you know about uk context?
cards.back: The Prophet’s migration from Makkah to Madinah (the Hijrah, 622 CE) marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. This event, commemorated every year by Muslims worldwide, symbolises the move from persecution to the establishment of a just community — a theme that resonates with British Muslims who value religious freedom and social justice.

cards.front: What should you know about uk context?
cards.back: In the UK, the Muslim and Christian communities often engage in interfaith dialogue about their respective views of Jesus. Organisations such as the Christian-Muslim Forum promote understanding by emphasising the shared reverence for Jesus while honestly acknowledging theological differences.
Adam (e.g. First human and first prophet; taught the name of all things; forgiven after eating from the tree)
Ibrahim (e.g. Friend of Allah (Khalilullah); rebuilt the Ka'bah; willing to sacrifice his son; model of faith)
Musa (e.g. Led the Israelites out of Egypt; received the Torah; spoke directly to Allah)
Isa (e.g. Born of the virgin Maryam; performed miracles; a prophet NOT the Son of God; will return before the Day of Judgement)
Muhammad (e.g. Final prophet; received the Qur'an; perfect model of how to live (Sunnah))

Students often confuse Sunni and Shi'a beliefs about predestination. Wrong: "All Muslims believe everything is predestined and humans have no free will." Correct: "Most Muslims believe God has foreknowledge but humans have free will to choose; the balance between predestination and free will is understood differently across traditions."
